result: Early ART during hyperacute infection significantly reduced peak plasma viral load (p<0.0001) compared to untreated infection, with median values of 4.18 vs 7.06 log copies/ml.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the manuscript 'links the timing of ART with the kinetics of total and intact proviral HIV DNA' with 'compelling' evidence. Reviewer 2 confirms 'early antiretroviral treatment restricts reservoir size' and notes the study shows 'rapid evolution and extensive immune selection' are reduced. Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'starting HIV treatment very early after infection...substantially reduces the peak viral load detectable (compared to untreated infection).'

result: Early ART did not prevent initial reservoir seeding, as total HIV-1 DNA levels at peak viremia were similar between early treated and untreated groups (p=0.104), confirming that the viral reservoir is established at the earliest stages of infection.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. Reviewer 2 states 'early antiretroviral treatment restricts reservoir size' but acknowledges the data show initial seeding occurs. Reviewer 3 explicitly confirms 'starting treatment early didn't reduce the amount of HIV DNA at the outset,' directly supporting this claim. No reviewer questions the statistical finding or interpretation.

result: Over one year of treatment, early ART resulted in a significant decline in total HIV-1 DNA (p=0.0004), while late ART did not reduce total proviral load. After one year, the early treated group had 1.3 times lower total proviral DNA compared to the chronic treated group (p=0.02).
evaluation: All reviewers affirm this longitudinal finding. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'early treatment was shown to be associated with a more rapid rate of decay in proviral genomes...over a period of one year post-treatment.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'starting treatment early...did lead to a gradual decrease in total HIV DNA quantity over time. In contrast, those who started treatment later didn't see much change in this parameter.' The statistical findings are not questioned.

result: The proportion of intact genomes after 1 year differed by treatment timing: 31% in untreated, 14% in late treated, and 0% in early treated groups. Intact genomes persisted after chronic treatment but were undetectable at the sampling depth after early ART.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical limitation: 'While it is indicated that intact genomes were not detected after one year following early treatment initiation, sampling depth is noted as a limitation of the study by the authors, and caution should thus be taken with interpretation where sequence numbers are low. Defective genomes are more abundant than intact genomes and are therefore more likely to be sampled.' This indicates the 0% finding may reflect sampling limitations rather than true absence, making the result uncertain despite being statistically significant.

result: Early treatment was associated with faster decay rates of both intact (51% per month) and defective (35% per month) proviral genomes compared to late treatment (13% and 3.4% per month respectively), suggesting more effective immune clearance from preserved immune function.
evaluation: All reviewers affirm this decay kinetics finding. Reviewer 2 states 'early treatment was shown to be associated with a more rapid rate of decay in proviral genomes, regardless of intactness, over a period of one year post-treatment.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'Starting treatment early led to a faster decrease in intact provirus (a measure of replication-competence), compared to starting treatment later.' The mechanistic interpretation about immune function is accepted without challenge.

result: Early ART reduced phylogenetic diversity of intact genomes (median pairwise distance 0.12% vs 0.48%, p=0.04) and minimized CTL escape mutations in Gag, Pol, and Nef epitopes compared to late treatment, which retained escape mutations particularly in the TW10 gag epitope.
evaluation: All reviewers affirm this finding. Reviewer 2 states 'Early treatment was also associated with reduced proviral diversity and fewer instances of polymorphisms associated with cytotoxic T-lymphocyte immune selection.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'early treatment reduced genetic diversity of the viral DNA and resulted in fewer immune escape variants within intact genomes.' The statistical findings and interpretation are not questioned by any reviewer.

result: Defective proviruses dominated the reservoir (65% of total), accumulating rapidly during infection with large internal deletions being the most common defect (77-79%). The proviral landscape in untreated and late treated participants was dominated by defective viruses, suggesting prolonged viral replication leads to defective genome accumulation.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this characterization of the defective proviral landscape. Reviewer 2 confirms 'early antiretroviral treatment restricts reservoir size, but further show that this restriction extends to defective viral genomes, where late treatment initiation was associated with a greater frequency of defective genomes.' Reviewer 3 notes the study evaluated 'various characteristics of the genetic makeup of the virus (intact/defective proviral genome)' with state-of-the-art methods. No concerns are raised about these findings.

result: Clonal expansion was detected in 27% of chronic treated and 30% of acute treated participants, occurring as early as 1 day post-detectable viremia in subtype C infection. The data suggest clonal expansion of intact genomes may be more likely with early treatment, though this requires cautious interpretation due to limited data.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly raises concerns: 'The analysis on clonal expansion of proviral genomes may be limited by higher sequence homogeneity in hyperacute infection i.e., cells with different proviral integration sites may have a higher likelihood of containing identical genomes compared to chronic infection.' The authors themselves note the data is 'limited and needs to be interpreted with caution,' indicating uncertainty about this finding.

result: Host and viral characteristics differentially impact reservoir maintenance depending on treatment timing. In acute treatment, only peak viral load associated with proviral DNA (p=0.02). In chronic treatment, baseline CD4 (p=0.002), peak viral load (p=0.03), and nadir CD4 (p<0.0001) were associated with proviral DNA levels.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these multivariate analysis findings without challenge. Reviewer 3 notes the study is 'well-designed' with 'appropriately selected' comparison groups, implicitly supporting the analytical approach. The statistical associations are not questioned by any reviewer, and the conclusion about host and viral characteristics is consistent with reviewer comments about the study's comprehensive approach.

result: This is the first longitudinal study in an African population examining HIV reservoir establishment in 35 women with subtype C infection, with 24 starting ART at median 1 day and 11 at median 456 days post-viremia onset. The study focused on women who are underrepresented in reservoir research.
evaluation: All reviewers strongly affirm the novelty and importance of the study population. Reviewer 1 states 'the importance of the work is high because the focus is on African women and clade C virus, both of which are understudied in the HIV reservoir field.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'A particular strength of this study is that it reports on reservoir characteristics in African women, a significantly understudied population.' Reviewer 3 notes 'particularly as the study was conducted in HIV-1 subtype C infected women (more cure studies have focussed on men and with subtype B infection).'

result: Early ART may accelerate reservoir clearance when combined with other interventional strategies, though early ART alone may not be sufficient to eradicate the persisting viral reservoir.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this speculative conclusion as appropriately qualified. Reviewer 2 states the findings 'points to an additional benefit of early treatment in the context of immune therapies to restrict the reservoir' and notes it 'provides clues to curative strategies.' Reviewer 3 confirms the findings 'are all features that are likely to facilitate more effective clearance of viral reservoir, especially when combined with other intervention strategies.' The cautious framing is appropriate and accepted.
